# Source and attribution restrictions

Assess the complete supplied recording on the exact motion “Is God real?”. William Lane Craig is pro (Theism); Michael Tooley is con (Atheism). The source description dates this UNC Charlotte event March 24, 2010. Assessment uses public English automatic captions only; no direct audio listening or paid transcription has occurred.

The motion does not silently become Christianity, biblical inerrancy, naturalism, or the existence of any supernatural cause. The speakers explicitly disagree about the relevant conception of God: Tooley defines an omnipotent, omniscient, morally perfect personal creator at 30:36 onward; Craig subsequently invokes a minimal creator concept and a cumulative case. Preserve their actual definitions and burdens as part of the exchange. Neither side's contested definition is automatically settled by the controller.

Formal rounds are Craig opening 08:51–29:41 (microphone restart until 09:30), Tooley opening 30:08–50:54, Craig first rebuttal 51:16–1:03:51, Tooley first rebuttal 1:04:19–1:16:17, Craig second rebuttal 1:16:49–1:25:15, Tooley second rebuttal 1:25:33–1:33:24, Craig closing 1:33:54–1:39:28, and Tooley closing 1:39:52–1:45:07. Audience questions begin after 1:46:47. Each named addressee answers, then the other receives a counter-response. Review the entire remainder through Craig's final probability reply around 2:16:19; the trailing word “failure” shares an event with moderator logistics at 2:16:44 and must not be extended into moderator speech. The event near 1:39:52 also carries the preceding closing word “philosopher” before Tooley begins; isolate each speaker's own claim.

Introductory biographies, moderator jokes and timekeeping, audience questions and applause are unscored context. Primary-speaker answers and responses are included. No primary-speaker scope exception or formal-rounds-only exclusion is used. Any newly discovered independent host advocacy or unresolved ownership must be reported before judgment.

Automatic captions repeatedly corrupt Tooley's name, Ratio Christi, technical names such as Carnap, Walley, Plantinga and Gaunilo, and terms such as inerrancy, a priori, prima facie and equiprobability. Do not treat these recognition artifacts as misnaming, incoherence, wrong citations, or participant mistakes. Preserve quotations exactly and choose quote-eligible spans free of material corruption. Do not silently normalize the source into a new transcript.

Tooley explicitly advances a probabilistic argument and rejects the logical incompatibility version. Preserve “wrong in itself/other things equal” versus wrong all things considered, known versus unknown properties, and conditional assumption versus concession. Discussion of resurrecting Jesus or a supernatural cause is frequently hypothetical; a supposition is not an admitted fact. Mathematical notation in the captions is imperfect (including the expression one over n plus one); assess only the clear surrounding verbal claim and inferential structure unless any disputed exact formula is verified. Garbled negative wording about necessary existence or miracles must not become an alleged self-contradiction.

Religious experience, naturalistic ethics, historical claims and cited authorities should be assessed as presented, without importing outside evidence or the speakers' later commentary. Source-description metadata is identity evidence only. No external debate review belongs in a judgment packet. Below-high attribution or materially consequential unresolved wording requires an explicit audio-verification reason; high confidence cannot be assigned merely to avoid that requirement.

moves.description: A finite cosmic past and causal principle support a timeless, immaterial, extraordinarily powerful personal origin of spacetime beyond the physical universe itself.

moves.critique: Strongest feature: Tooley precisely distinguishes existential conclusions about a designer or first cause from the fuller attribute package at issue, preventing evidential support for some supernatural intelligence from silently becoming support for a perfectly good classical deity. moves.description: Life-permitting constants occupy an independently specified narrow range, making purposive cosmic design more plausible than necessity or undirected chance under the stated explanatory comparison.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig clearly organizes the inference around a narrow life-permitting range, the alleged absence of physically necessary values, and an independently recognizable biological specification, thereby presenting design as comparative explanation rather than simple astonishment. Principal limitation: The chance alternative cannot be assessed without a justified probability distribution over possible constants, while dismissing necessity and multiverse selection requires more scientific argument than the compressed presentation supplies. Live burden: Pro must show that design predicts these constants better than developed naturalistic competitors; con can weaken the inference by identifying an unjustified measure or an inadequately excluded rival without proving that fine-tuning has no evidential force.

moves.description: Tooley broadens causation beyond beginnings, arguing that divine states temporally related to creation would require prior causal conditions just as persisting physical states do.
moves.critique: Strongest feature: The electron example shows that causal explanation can concern a thing’s state at a time rather than only its coming into existence, directly challenging an artificially narrow causal vocabulary, because continued existence at a time can depend causally on an earlier state without beginning anew. moves.critique: Strongest feature: Craig clearly distinguishes the necessity of a conditional from necessity of its consequent and uses the infallible-barometer analogy to explain how knowledge can track an event without determining it, because a different free act would correspond to different divine knowledge rather than falsified knowledge.
